bull_case: Neutron and Iridium can turn the company from a supplier into an operator of space infrastructure and applications.
bear_case: SpaceX, large defense primes and well-funded constellation operators can respond aggressively, while Rocket Lab bears high execution risk.
thesis: Rocket Lab is evolving from a launch company into vertically integrated space infrastructure. The disruptive vector is not only Electron; it is the ability to design, manufacture, launch and eventually operate revenue-producing constellations under one stack.

evidence.claim: Rocket Lab completed 21 Electron launches in 2025.
Q2 backlog reached $2.36B and launch backlog exceeded 90 missions.
Iridium adds global network, spectrum and recurring applications revenue.

counterevidence: Rocket Lab remains cash-flow negative on a standalone basis and the Iridium transaction materially increases integration, financing and dilution complexity.
unknowns: Neutron commercial readiness and launch economics
Long-run dilution cadence and owner FCF/share conversion
falsifiers: A major Neutron delay, persistent launch failures, failure to close/integrate Iridium, or continued double-digit share dilution without per-share FCF progress would weaken the thesis.
next_checks: Neutron schedule, backlog conversion, post-close Iridium FCF, diluted share count, ATM usage

subscores.rationale: Electron lowered access-to-orbit friction for small payloads; vertical integration extends that cost/performance model across spacecraft and services.
21 Electron launches in 2025, Q2 revenue +62%, backlog +137%, and >90 launch backlog demonstrate scaled adoption.
Launch, spacecraft/components, optical systems, defense, Neutron, and Iridium applications create multiple adjacent value pools.

uncertainties.rationale: Rocket Lab remains in a high-investment, acquisition-heavy transition with large execution variance.
